s: Vitoria's De Indis lists, among the legitimate titles of Spanish presence in the Indies 'by reason of natural society and communication', a right to travel and live there and a right to trade (*ius commercii*) by importing goods the Indians lack and exporting their gold and silver, which Indian princes may not forbid.

src.loc: De Indis, summary of the legitimate titles; p. 358

src.loc: De Indis, summary of the legitimate titles; p. 358

s: Grotius (De iure belli ac pacis II.12.14) takes need as the most natural measure of a thing's worth, following Aristotle, but not the only one, since the will of men, 'mistress of things', desires many things beyond necessity, as luxury gave pearls their price.

src.l: Hugo Grotius, 1631, De iure belli ac pacis
src.q: Mensura ejus quod res quæque valeat maxime naturalis est indigentia, ut Aristoteles recte ostendit : quod in permutationibus rerum apud barbaros populos maxime spectatur. src.l: Hugo Grotius, 1631, De iure belli ac pacis
src.q: The most natural measure of what each thing is worth is need, as Aristotle rightly shows: which is observed most of all in the exchange of things among barbarian peoples. s: Grotius follows the jurist Paulus that prices are set not by individual affection or utility but 'commonly', so a thing is worth what is commonly offered or given for it, a price that always has some latitude unless law fixes a price 'in a point'.

src.l: Hugo Grotius, 1631, De iure belli ac pacis
src.q: Pretia rerum non ex affectu nec utilitate singulorum, sed communiter funguntur : id est, ut alibi explicat, quanti omnibus valeret.

s: Pegolotti's Pratica della mercatura (c. 1340) is a reference of place-by-place commercial facts: for Famagusta it records which goods sell by weight or by measure, in which coin, and how local units convert (saffron by the pound in white besants; rotoli, pesi, okke).

src.l: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti, 1766, Pratica della mercatura
src.q: Saffron is sold by the pound of weight and in white besants. It is handled in rotoli, and every rotolo is calculated as 6 pounds at 54 pesi , based on 79 pesi to a pound, and 44 pesi for one okka, with 12 okke making one rotolo.

s: Cotrugli derives trade from human multiplication and need: men found money as a universal medium valid in every time and place so as to obtain necessities without reciprocal barter, and 'from this, as from a living fountain', *mercatura* (trade) takes its beginning.

src.q: I divide exchange primarily into those two types: namely, "small exchange" and "exchange by letters"

s: Scaruffi's L'Alitinonfo (1582) proposes that the whole world keep accounts of coins under a single standard he calls the 'imperiale', and predicts bankers and calculators would soon make this reckoning common to every nation.

src.l: Gasparo Scaruffi, 1582, L'Alitinonfo

s: Davanzati's Lezione delle monete (1588; English 1696) explains prices by consent: all earthly things, which satisfy men's wants, are 'by the Consent of Nations' worth all the gold (with silver and copper) wrought in the world, so a part of the goods is worth the corresponding part of the gold.

src.l: Bernardo Davanzati, 1696, A Discourse upon Coins (trans. John Toland of Lezione delle monete)
src.q: Now all theſe by the Conſent of Nations are worth all the Gold (comprehending alſo the Silver and Copper) that is wrought in the World.

s: Davanzati allows the magistrate discretion over a coin's shape, stamp and name but not its substance: money may be coined only of the three metals and the pieces must contain fine metal answerable to their names, else the people are cheated.

src.l: Bernardo Davanzati, 1696, A Discourse upon Coins (trans. John Toland of Lezione delle monete)
src.q: he may coin no Money but of the three known Metals, nor set a false Price upon the Pieces, as it must needs happen, if, after trying of ’em, they should be found not to consist of fine Metal enough answerable to their Names.

s: Barbon (1690) says the value of all wares arises from their use, use being to supply the wants of body and mind; things of no use have no value.

src.l: Nicholas Barbon, 1690, A Discourse of Trade
src.q: THE Value of all Wares arise from their Use ; Things of no Use, have no Value, as the English Phrase is, They are good for nothing.

s: Barbon (1690) denies that a nation can be ruined by spending as a person can: a person's estate is finite but 'the Stock of a Nation Infinite', which neither thrift adds to nor prodigality diminishes.

src.l: Nicholas Barbon, 1690, A Discourse of Trade
src.q: This is true, of a Person, but not of a Nation; because his Estate is Finite, but the Stock of a Nation Infinite, and can never be consumed

s: Barbon (1690) lists among the benefits of trade that it 'hath occasioned Peace', making it more in mankind's interest to live at home in peace than to seek fortunes by war, half a century before Montesquieu's *doux commerce* (gentle commerce, which softens manners and keeps peace).

src.l: Nicholas Barbon, 1690, A Discourse of Trade
src.q: Another Benefit of Trade , is, That , it doth not only bring Plenty , but hath occasioned Peace

src.q: more the Interest of Mankind to live at home in Peace, than to seek their fortunes abroad by Wars.

s: Discourses upon Trade (1691) says the whole world as to trade is but as one nation, nations being as persons, so losing trade with one nation is a loss to the trade of the world.

src.l: Dudley North, 1691, Discourses upon Trade
src.q: That the whole World as to Trade, is but as one Nation or People, and therein Nations are as Persons.

s: The same preface (1691) argues there can be no trade unprofitable to the public, because if any proves so men leave it off: an early self-correcting mechanism with no official in it.

src.l: Dudley North, 1691, Discourses upon Trade
src.q: That there can be no Trade unprofitable to the Publick; for if any prove so, men leave it off

s: In XX.2 Montesquieu says the natural effect of commerce is peace, because trading nations become mutually dependent, but that the spirit of commerce which unites nations does not unite individuals: where it alone reigns, every human action and moral virtue is trafficked.

src.l: Montesquieu, 1851, De l'esprit des lois
src.q: L'effet naturel du commerce est de porter à la paix.

src.l: Montesquieu, 1851, De l'esprit des lois
src.q: Mais, si l'esprit de commerce unit les nations, il n'unit pas de même les particuliers.

src.l: David Hume, 1898, Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary, vol. 1 (Green & Grose)
src.q: The greatness of a state, and the happiness of its subjects, how independent soever they maybe supposed in some respects

s: In Of the Jealousy of Trade (1758) Hume calls groundless the habit of treating all trading states as rivals who can flourish only at one's expense, and declares that not only as a man but as a British subject he prays for the flourishing commerce of Germany, Spain, Italy and even France.

src.l: David Hume, 1898, Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary, vol. 1 (Green & Grose)
src.loc: Of the Jealousy of Trade, p. 345 [scan 353]
src.q: to consider all trading states as their rivals, and to suppose that it is impossible for any of them to flourish, but at their expence.

src.l: David Hume, 1898, Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary, vol. 1 (Green & Grose)
src.loc: Of the Jealousy of Trade, p. 348 [scan 356]
src.q: not only as a man, but as a BRITISH subject, I pray for the flourishing commerce of GERMANY, SPAIN, ITALY, and even FRANCE itself.

s: Quesnay's maxims (as printed in the Oncken edition) say the surest and most profitable *police* (the regulation and good order of a state's trade and provisioning) of internal and external commerce consists in full liberty of competition.

src.l: François Quesnay, August Oncken (ed.), 1888, Oeuvres économiques et philosophiques
src.q: la police du commerce intérieure et extérieure la plus sûre, la plus exacte, la plus profitable à l'état et à la nation consiste dans la pleine liberté de la concurrence.

s: The Tableau's own explanation supposes a kingdom whose agriculture is brought to perfection and 'maintained by full liberty of commerce and entire security' of farming capital; the circular flow is a model of reproduction under a policy, not a claim that the economy regulates itself.

src.l: François Quesnay, August Oncken (ed.), 1888, Oeuvres économiques et philosophiques
src.q: On suppose un grand royaume dont la culture portée à sa perfection et entretenue par une pleine liberté de commerce et par une entière sûreté des richesses d'exploitation, donne un revenu de cinq milliards.

s: Mercier de la Rivière (1767) writes that when each man is free to enlarge the enjoyments he can offer others in order to enlarge those he receives, 'the world then goes by itself', desire and liberty of enjoyment endlessly provoking more production and more industry.

src.l: Pierre-Paul Mercier de la Rivière, 1767, L'ordre naturel et essentiel des sociétés politiques
src.q: Le monde alors va de lui-même; le desir de jouïr & la liberté de jouïr ne cessant de provoquer la multiplication des productions & l'accroissement de l'industrie

s: Du Pont's Physiocratie (1767) holds that the natural order of commerce suggests no motive for war and no reservation in peace treaties; trade wars can only serve a monopoly.

src.l: Pierre Samuel Du Pont de Nemours (ed.), 1767, Physiocratie, ou Constitution naturelle du gouvernement
src.q: l'ordre naturel du commerce, lequel ne suggere aucun motif de guerre, ni aucune réserve dans les traités de paix.

s: Turgot (written 1766) states that the workman's wage is limited by competition among those who work for subsistence, so that he only gains a livelihood.

src.l: Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot, 1793, Reflections on the Formation and Distribution of Wealth
src.q: The wages of the workman is limited by the competition among thofe who work for a fubfiftence. He only gains a livelihood.

s: Ferguson (1767) says nations stumble upon establishments that are the result of human action but not the execution of any human design.

src.l: Adam Ferguson, 1767, An Essay on the History of Civil Society
src.q: nations stumble upon establishments, which are indeed the result of human action, but not the execution of any human design

s: Steuart (1767) addresses political oeconomy to a statesman who, knowing his territory, may 'lay down his plan of political oeconomy' and distribute the inhabitants as his judgment alone decides.

src.l: James Steuart, 1767, An Inquiry into the Principles of Political Oeconomy, vol. 1
src.q: he may lay down his plan of political oeconomy, and chalk out a distribution of inhabitants, as if the number were already compleat. It will depend upon his judgment alone

s: In his Glasgow lectures (c. 1763) Smith concludes that 'it is by far the best police to leave things to their natural course' (*police*: the regulation of trade and provisioning), with no bounties or taxes on commodities, and derives the division of labour from a propensity to barter known to no other animal.

src.l: Adam Smith, Edwin Cannan (ed.), 1896, Lectures on Justice, Police, Revenue and Arms
src.q: Upon the whole, therefore, it is by far the best police to leave things to their natural course, and allow no bounties, nor impose taxes on commodities.

src.l: Adam Smith, Edwin Cannan (ed.), 1896, Lectures on Justice, Police, Revenue and Arms
src.q: it flows from a direct propensity in human nature for one man to barter with another, which is common to all men, and known to no other animal.

s: Smith (WN I.i, 1776) describes pin-making divided into about eighteen distinct operations and a small manufactory where ten men made far more than they could separately.

src.l: Adam Smith, 1776, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (Books I-III)
src.q: where ten men only were employed, and where some of them consequently performed two or three distinct operations.

s: Smith (WN I.ii) says the division of labour is not the effect of human wisdom foreseeing its utility but the slow consequence of a propensity in human nature to truck, barter and exchange.

src.l: Adam Smith, 1776, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (Books I-III)
src.q: the propensity to truck, barter, and exchange one thing for another.

src.l: Adam Smith, 1776, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (Books I-III)
src.q: It is the necessary, though very slow and gradual consequence of a certain propensity in human nature which has in view no such extensive utility

s: Smith (WN I.ii) says we expect our dinner not from the benevolence of the butcher, brewer or baker but from their regard to their own interest, addressing their self-love rather than their humanity.

src.l: Adam Smith, 1776, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (Books I-III)
src.q: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.

s: In WN IV.ii (1776) the individual who prefers domestic to foreign *industry* (labour employed) for his own security, and directs it for his own gain, is 'led by an invisible hand to promote an end which was no part of his intention', the annual revenue of the society.

src.l: Adam Smith, 1776, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
Adam Smith, 1776, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations

s: Condillac (1776) founds the value of things on their utility, that is on our need of them, so that value grows with scarcity and falls with abundance.

src.l: Étienne Bonnot de Condillac, 1776, Le Commerce et le gouvernement considérés relativement l'un à l'autre
src.q: La valeur des choses est fondée sur leur utilité, sur le besoin que nous en avons, ou sur l'usage que nous pouvons en faire.

src.l: Étienne Bonnot de Condillac, 1776, Le Commerce et le gouvernement considérés relativement l'un à l'autre
src.q: La valeur des choses croît donc dans la rareté

s: Condillac (1776) says the price of money in trading places is set by the altercations of borrowers and lenders, and asks why a government that admits it has no business fixing the prices of things sold at market should fix interest.

src.l: Étienne Bonnot de Condillac, 1776, Le Commerce et le gouvernement considérés relativement l'un à l'autre
src.q: Le Gouvernement reconnoît qu'il ne lui appartient pas de faire des Loix pour fixer le prix des choses qui se vendent au Marché

s: Rothschild (Economic Sentiments, 2001), as summarised in a review abstract, argues that Smith as the prophet of *laissez-faire* ('let them do': leave trade free of regulation) and an optimal *invisible hand* is a myth: his economics cannot be separated from his political philosophy and his idea of freedom differs from modern liberal economics.

src.l: Roger E. Backhouse, 2002, Economic Sentiments: Adam Smith, Condorcet, and the Enlightenment (review of E. Rothschild, 2001)

s: Bacon (Novum Organum I.81, 1620) says the sciences have failed because their goal was never fixed, and names the true goal as endowing human life with new inventions and resources, against the crowd who seek knowledge only for profit or reputation.

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1779, Novum Organum Scientiarum (Latin ed.)
src.q: The true and legitimate goal of the sciences is none other than this: that human life be endowed with new inventions and resources.
src.qo: Me- ta autem scientiarum vera & legitima, non alia est, quam ut dotetur vita humana novis inventis, & copiis.

s: Bacon (Novum Organum I.129, 1620) cites printing, gunpowder and the nautical compass, inventions unknown to the ancients, as having changed the face and state of things throughout the world more than any empire, sect or star.

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1779, Novum Organum Scientiarum (Latin ed.)
src.q: the art of printing, gunpowder, and the nautical compass. For these three have changed the face and state of things throughout the world

s: Bacon's New Atlantis (written c. 1624, printed 1627) gives Salomon's House the end of 'the Knowledge of Causes, and Secret Motions of Things; and the Enlarging of the bounds of Humane Empire, to the Effecting of all Things possible': an open-ended, state-endowed research institution.

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1631, New Atlantis (appended to Sylva Sylvarum, 1631 ed.)
src.loc: New Atlantis p. 30 (scan 318), Sylva Sylvarum 1631 ed.
src.q: The End of our Foundation is the Knowledge of Causes, and Secret Motions of Things; and the Enlarging of the bounds of Humane Empire, to the Effecting of all Things possible.

s: The Statute of Monopolies (1624) voids monopolies generally but exempts letters patent of fourteen years or under for 'the sole working or making of any manner of new manufactures' granted to 'the true and first inventor', provided they do not raise prices at home or hurt trade.

src.l: Parliament of England, 1624, Statute of Monopolies (21 Jac. I c. 3)

s: Hartlib's Legacy of Husbandry (1651; 1655 ed. read) lists agricultural trials as 'Experiments and Improvements', pairing 'Improvement' with experiment and with a new invention or engine for enriching land.

src.l: Samuel Hartlib, 1655, Samuel Hartlib His Legacy of Husbandry (3rd ed.)
src.q: Experiments and Improvements for inriching of land by Mr. Plats New Invention or Engine

s: Sprat (History of the Royal Society, 1667) says the Society resolves to compile histories of all trades, great and small, and to publish them, expecting that when the secrets of manufactures are described it will be seen how far the crafts may be 'promoted'.

src.l: Thomas Sprat, 1667, The History of the Royal Society of London
src.q: they reſolve to proceed, till they have not only obtain'd an Account of all the Great, and moſt ſubſtantial Trades

src.l: Thomas Sprat, 1667, The History of the Royal Society of London
src.q: if they found any more such Tradesmen, they should be sure to admit them all, without any more ado

s: Sprat (1667) argues that the country with most manufactures is richest, that men's labour is true riches, and that saving hands by inventions and applying them to other works will increase those riches, with vent abroad if not at home.

src.l: Thomas Sprat, 1667, The History of the Royal Society of London
src.q: That Country is ſtill the richeſt and moſt powerful, which entertains moſt Manufa-ctures. The hands of men employ'd are true Riches: The ſaving of thoſe hands by inventions of Art, and applying them to other Works, will increaſe thoſe Riches.

s: Smith (Wealth of Nations I.viii, 1776) says the labouring poor are happiest while a society advances towards, not when it has acquired, its 'full complement of riches': the progressive state is cheerful, the stationary dull, the declining melancholy.

src.l: Adam Smith, 1776, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
src.q: The progressive state is in reality the chearful and the hearty state to all the different orders of the society.  The stationary is dull; the declining, melancholy.

s: Malthus (Essay, 1798, ch. 1) frames the question of the age as whether man will advance towards 'illimitable, and hitherto unconceived improvement' or be condemned to perpetual oscillation between happiness and misery, and argues for the second.

src.l: Thomas Robert Malthus, 1798, An Essay on the Principle of Population (1st ed.)

s: Ricardo (Principles ch. 7, 1817) shows that Portugal may import English cloth even though she could make it with less labour, because employing her capital in wine buys more cloth than she could make: the case later called comparative advantage.

src.l: David Ricardo, 1817, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (later ed. with section numbers, incl. ch. 31 of 1821)
src.q: This exchange might even take place, notwithstanding that the commodity imported by Portugal could be produced there with less labour than in England.

s: Ricardo (Principles ch. 6, 1817) holds that profits naturally tend to fall as more labour is needed for additional food, a 'gravitation' checked only at intervals by improvements in machinery and discoveries in agriculture.

src.l: David Ricardo, 1817, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (later ed. with section numbers, incl. ch. 31 of 1821)
src.q: This tendency, this gravitation as it were of profits, is happily checked at repeated intervals by

src.l: David Ricardo, 1817, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (later ed. with section numbers, incl. ch. 31 of 1821)
src.q: the improvements in machinery, connected with the pro- duction of necessaries, as well as by discoveries in the science of agriculture

s: Ricardo (1817, ch. 5 on the poor laws) writes of England's 'period of progressive prosperity' and of the *stationary state* 'from which I trust we are yet far distant': he expects it, but not soon.

src.l: David Ricardo, 1817, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (later ed. with section numbers, incl. ch. 31 of 1821)
src.q: if we should attain the stationary state, from which I trust we are yet far distant

s: Ricardo (ch. 31 'On Machinery', added 1821) retracts his earlier view that machinery benefits all classes: he is now 'convinced' that substituting machinery for labour is often very injurious to labourers, because net revenue can rise while the gross fund that maintains labour falls.

src.l: David Ricardo, 1817, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (later ed. with section numbers, incl. ch. 31 of 1821)
src.q: I am convinced, that the substitution of machinery for human labour, is often very injurious to the interests of the class of labourers.

s: Say (Traité, 1803; 1821 English of the 4th ed. read) answers 'adventurers in the different channels of industry' who blame lack of vent: since products are bought with other products, 'it is production which opens a demand for products' (the loi des débouchés).

src.l: Jean-Baptiste Say, 1821, A Treatise on Political Economy (tr. C. R. Prinsep from the 4th French ed.)
src.q: It is common to hear adventurers in the different channels of industry assert, that their difficulty lies, not in the production, but in the disposal of commodities

src.l: Jean-Baptiste Say, 1821, A Treatise on Political Economy (tr. C. R. Prinsep from the 4th French ed.)
src.q: Which leads us to a conclusion, that may at first sight appear paradoxical; viz. that it is production which opens a demand for products.

s: Sismondi (Nouveaux principes, preface to 2nd ed., 1827) charges that Say and Ricardo came to believe consumption an unlimited power, bounded only by production, announced that all wealth produced would find consumers, and so encouraged the glut of markets that 'today' distresses the civilised world.

src.l: J.-C.-L. Simonde de Sismondi, 1827, Nouveaux principes d'économie politique, 2nd ed., vol. 1
src.loc: Preface to the 2nd ed., pp. xli–xlii

s: Carlyle ('Signs of the Times', 1829) names his era 'the Mechanical Age', the 'Age of Machinery, in every outward and inward sense of that word', where nothing is done directly but by rule and calculated contrivance.

src.l: Thomas Carlyle, 1829, Signs of the Times (Edinburgh Review)
src.loc: Edinburgh Review 1829, para. 'Were we required to characterise this age'

s: Babbage (Economy of Machinery, 1832, §226; restated 1864) adds to Smith's causes of the gains from division of labour the one he thought most important: by splitting work into processes of different skill and force, the master buys exactly the quantity of each that each process needs.

src.l: Charles Babbage, 1864, Passages from the Life of a Philosopher
src.q: By dividing the work to be executed into different processes, each requiring different degrees of skill, or of force, the master manufacturer can purchase exactly that precise quantity of both which is necessary for each process.

src.l: Charles Babbage, 1832, On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures

s: Babbage (1832, §241) argues that the division of labour applies 'with equal success to mental as to mechanical operations', illustrated by Prony's division of the French logarithm-table calculations.

src.l: Charles Babbage, 1832, On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures

s: Ure (Philosophy of Manufactures, 1835) describes the factory principle as withdrawing every delicate process from the 'ignorance and waywardness of workmen' and placing it under self-acting machinery, and calls the factory system Arkwright's, possibly 'an inevitable step in the social progression of the world'.

src.l: Andrew Ure, 1835, The Philosophy of Manufactures
Andrew Ure, 1835, The Philosophy of Manufactures

s: List (Das nationale System, 1841) says the loss from protective tariffs is only in values, while the nation gains powers by which it can produce incalculable sums of value 'for eternal times': the loss is the price of the nation's industrial education.

src.l: Friedrich List, 1910, Das nationale System der politischen Ökonomie (reprint)
src.q: dagegen gewinnt sie Kräfte, vermittels welcher sie für ewige Zeiten in den Stand gesetzt wird, unberechenbare Summen von Werten zu produzieren. Dieser Aufwand an Werten ist demnach nur als der Preis der industriellen Erziehung der Nation zu betrachten.

s: Carlyle (Past and Present, 1843) holds that 'Laissez-faire', 'Supply-and-demand' and 'Cash-payment for the sole nexus' were not and never will be a practicable law of union for a society of men.

src.l: Thomas Carlyle, 1843, Past and Present
src.loc: Book I, ch. 'Gospel of Mammonism' region (Gutenberg text)

s: Bastiat (Economic Sophisms, 1845, ch. 20) holds that machine-breaking and the prohibition of foreign goods rest on the same doctrine, and calls inconsistent those who applaud inventions yet keep protection.

src.l: Frédéric Bastiat, 1845, Economic Sophisms (English tr.)
src.loc: ch. XX 'Human Labour, National Labour', p. 87 (scan 100)
src.q: MACHINE-BREAKING—prohibition of foreign commodities—are two acts founded on the same doctrine.

s: Mill (Principles IV.vi, 1848) says political economists have always seen that the increase of wealth is not boundless and that the *stationary state* lies at the end of the progressive state; he adds that a stationary condition of capital and population implies no stationary state of human improvement.

src.l: John Stuart Mill, 1848, Principles of Political Economy, vol. II
src.q: It must always have been seen, more or less distinctly, by political economists, that the increase of wealth is not boundless; that at the end of what they term the progressive state lies the stationary state

src.l: John Stuart Mill, 1848, Principles of Political Economy, vol. II
src.q: a stationary condition of capital and population implies no stationary state of human improvement

s: Marx (Kapital I, 1867, ch. 4) distinguishes the circulation of commodities C–M–C, selling in order to buy, from a second, specifically different form M–C–M, buying in order to sell, which is the circulation of money as capital.

src.l: Karl Marx, 1867, Das Kapital. Kritik der politischen Oekonomie. Erster Band
src.q: Neben dieser Form finden wir aber eine zweite, spezifisch unterschiedene vor, die Form G — W — G, Verwandlung von Geld in Waare und Rückverwandlung von Waare in Geld, kaufen um zu verkaufen.

s: Marx (Kapital I, 1867, ch. 13) says Ure likes to present the central machine of the factory 'not only as an automaton but as an autocrat', and distinguishes machinery as such from its capitalist application in the modern factory system.

src.l: Karl Marx, 1867, Das Kapital. Kritik der politischen Oekonomie. Erster Band
src.q: Ure liebt es daher auch die Centralmaschine, von der die Bewegung ausgeht, nicht nur als Automat, sondern als Autokrat darzustellen.

s: Read together, Smith (1776), Malthus (1798), Ricardo (1817) and Mill (1848) all keep a *stationary state* (where wealth and population stop growing) as the horizon of accumulation, with *improvement* (making land and work yield more) as a repeated postponement; the texts in this slice that frame growth as open-ended are Bacon (power over nature), Sprat (labour-saving), Say (no general glut) and List (productive powers 'for eternal times'), none of them classical-Ricardian.

src.l: John Stuart Mill, 1848, Principles of Political Economy, vol. II
src.q: that all progress in wealth is but a postponement of this

src.l: David Ricardo, 1817, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (later ed. with section numbers, incl. ch. 31 of 1821)
src.q: This tendency, this gravitation as it were of profits

s: Mokyr (2005) traces the intellectual origins of the Industrial Revolution to the seventeenth-century Baconian programme of expanding useful knowledge, carried out by eighteenth-century Enlightenment institutions; without the Enlightenment the IR could not have become sustained growth. Thesis: ideas-first.

src.l: Joel Mokyr, 2005, The Intellectual Origins of Modern Economic Growth

s: Mokyr's Enlightened Economy (2009) argues, per its publisher abstract, that intellectual rather than material forces drove Britain's transformation between the Glorious Revolution and the Great Exhibition, above all the Enlightenment's belief in progress and science. Thesis: ideas-first.

src.l: Joel Mokyr, 2009, The Enlightened Economy: Britain and the Industrial Revolution, 1700-1850

s: McCloskey argues that the virtues of a bourgeois life enabled capitalist development (Bourgeois Virtues, 2006, abstract), and in Bourgeois Dignity (2010) that a change in the esteem and rhetoric accorded to trade and betterment, not economics, explains the modern world. Thesis: rhetoric-first.

src.l: Deirdre Nansen McCloskey, 2006, The Bourgeois Virtues
Deirdre Nansen McCloskey, 2010, Bourgeois Dignity: Why Economics Can't Explain the Modern World

s: Allen (2009) argues the British IR was a response to the global economy: wages were high and capital and energy cheap in Britain, so the steam engine, the cotton mill and coal in metallurgy were uniquely profitable to invent and use there. Thesis: prices-first.

src.l: Robert C. Allen, 2009, The British Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective

s: North and Weingast (1989) argue that the constitutional settlement after 1688 let the English Crown commit credibly to secure property rights and non-confiscation, with capital-market evidence of success. Thesis: institutions-first.

src.l: Douglass C. North, Barry R. Weingast, 1989, Constitutions and Commitment: The Evolution of Institutions Governing Public Choice in Seventeenth-Century England

s: De Vries (1994) proposes an 'industrious revolution' preceding the IR: a household-level reallocation that raised both the supply of marketed labour and goods and the demand for market-supplied goods, a demand-side change before the supply-side IR. Thesis: demand-side.

src.l: Jan de Vries, 1994, The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution

s: Slack (2014) argues the idea of *improvement*, gradual and cumulative betterment, and the word itself, were new in seventeenth-century England, became a slogan for agriculture, industry, commerce and welfare, and had no equivalent in other languages. Thesis: ideas-first, dated to the 17th century and to information.

src.l: Paul Slack, 2014, The Invention of Improvement: Information and Material Progress in Seventeenth-Century England

s: Hirschman (1977) reconstructs how the pursuit of material interest, long condemned as avarice, was assigned the role of containing the destructive passions in 17th–18th-century argument, stressing continuity rather than a Marxian or Weberian break. Thesis: ideas/rhetoric (legitimation), pre-capitalist.

src.l: Albert O. Hirschman, 1977, The Passions and the Interests: Political Arguments for Capitalism before Its Triumph

s: Jacob (1997) explains how scientific knowledge became integral to European culture in the 17th–18th centuries and how this led to the IR, and why England made the transition more successfully than the Continent. Thesis: ideas-first (applied Newtonian science).

src.l: Margaret C. Jacob, 1997, Scientific Culture and the Making of the Industrial West

s: Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014) attribute Britain's lead to the quality of its labour force: British workers c. 1750 were physically and mechanically superior, so inventions from anywhere were adopted faster there; they read high wages as a sign of this quality. Thesis: human-capital (skills) first.

src.l: Morgan Kelly, Joel Mokyr, Cormac Ó Gráda, 2014, Precocious Albion: A New Interpretation of the British Industrial Revolution

s: Against Allen's prices-first account, Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014) treat Britain's high wages as consistent with higher labour quality rather than as the factor price that made machines profitable; Humphries also contested Allen's high-wage evidence (answered in Allen 2014).

src.l: Morgan Kelly, Joel Mokyr, Cormac Ó Gráda, 2014, Precocious Albion: A New Interpretation of the British Industrial Revolution
Robert C. Allen, 2014, The high wage economy and the industrial revolution: a restatement

s: Clark (2007) explicitly counters the prevailing theory that the IR was sparked by the sudden development of stable political and legal institutions, arguing instead for slow cultural (behavioural) change.

src.l: Gregory Clark, 2007, A Farewell to Alms: A Brief Economic History of the World

s: The brief's opposition 'Slack's 17th-century improvement versus Mokyr's 18th-century Enlightenment' is overstated: Mokyr's 2005 abstract itself traces the IR's origins to the 17th-century Baconian programme. The real difference is where the causal weight sits: Slack on an English culture and information order of the 1600s, Mokyr on 18th-century Enlightenment institutions that diffused useful knowledge.

src.l: Joel Mokyr, 2005, The Intellectual Origins of Modern Economic Growth
Paul Slack, 2014, The Invention of Improvement: Information and Material Progress in Seventeenth-Century England

s: Aquinas holds that the just price (*pretium iustum*) is not fixed to a point but lies within a range set by estimation, so a small excess or shortfall does not break the equality of justice; only a notable loss must be compensated.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1887, Summa Theologica, Tomus Tertius: Secunda Secundae
src.loc: ST II-II q.77 a.1 resp., p. 369 [scan 385]
src.q: the just price of things is not determined down to a point

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1887, Summa Theologica, Tomus Tertius: Secunda Secundae
src.loc: ST II-II q.77 a.1 resp., p. 370 [scan 386]
src.q: consists in a certain estimation; so that a slight addition or subtraction does not seem to destroy the equality of justice
src.qo: dam æstimatione consistit; ita quod modica additio vel minutio non videtur tollere æqualitatem justitiæ.

s: Aquinas says the price of saleable things is not reckoned by their rank in nature (a horse may be worth more than a slave) but by how they serve human use.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1887, Summa Theologica, Tomus Tertius: Secunda Secundae
src.loc: ST II-II q.77 a.2 ad 3, p. 371 [scan 387]
src.q: is considered according to how the things serve human use
src.qo: sed consideratur secundum quod res in usum hominis veniunt.

s: In Aquinas's case of a seller who knows more merchants are coming (so prices will fall), selling at the price he finds is not unjust and he need not disclose it; disclosing would be supererogatory virtue, not a debt of justice.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1887, Summa Theologica, Tomus Tertius: Secunda Secundae
src.loc: ST II-II q.77 a.3 ad 4, p. 372 [scan 388]
src.q: a seller who sells a thing according to the current market price he finds does not seem to act against justice if he does not explain what is to come
src.qo: unde venditor qui vendit rem secundum pretium quod invenit, non videtur contra justitiam facere, si quod futurum est non exponat.

s: Aquinas holds that *negotiatio* (trading: buying in order to sell dearer) considered in itself has a certain baseness (*turpitudo*), because by its nature it serves the endless desire for gain rather than an honest or necessary end.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1887, Summa Theologica, Tomus Tertius: Secunda Secundae
src.loc: ST II-II q.77 a.4 resp., p. 373 [scan 389]
src.q: trading considered in itself has a certain baseness
src.qo: negotiatio secundum se considerata quamdam turpitudinem habet

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1887, Summa Theologica, Tomus Tertius: Secunda Secundae
src.loc: ST II-II q.77 a.4 resp., p. 373 [scan 389]
src.q: negotiatio secundum se considerata quamdam turpitudinem habet

s: Aquinas makes trade lawful when moderate gain is ordered to a further end (supporting a household, helping the needy, supplying the country with necessities) and sought 'as a stipend for labour'; a seller who improves a thing earns the reward of his labour.

s: Ibn Khaldun calls the dynasty and sultanate 'the great market' of the nation, the source of all lesser markets: when the ruler hoards revenue instead of spending it, purchases fall, markets slacken and tax receipts drop.

s: Ibn Khaldun argues that a ruler who trades or farms for revenue harms his subjects: merchants and cultivators of roughly equal means compete with one another, but cannot compete with the sovereign's far larger capital, and prices rise.

s: Ibn Khaldun holds that among civilised people gain and livelihood (kasb, rizq) represent the value of human labour, and that the price of a product, even of grain, contains the value of the labour put into it, though people often fail to notice it.

s: Franco and Nickl (2018) read Olivi's Tractatus de contractibus (c. 1293-95) as combining a subject-based theory of value, a just-price theory and a systematic concept of capitale: money destined to trade carries a 'seminal' added value, so a price may compensate the owner's forgone use of capital.

src.l: Giuseppe Franco, Peter Nickl, 2018, A Certain Seminal Character of Profit which We Commonly Call 'Capital': Peter of John Olivi and the Tractatus de contractibus

s: De Roover (1958) argues that the view of the just price as a pious construct set apart from supply and demand is a 'fairy tale', and that for the scholastics the just price was in general the current market price.

s: Koehn and Wilbratte (2012) reject both the cost-of-production and the market-price readings of Aquinas's just price, arguing it is the price a just person would agree to, weighing the parties' well-being and the common good.

src.l: Daryl Koehn, Barry J. Wilbratte, 2012, A Defense of a Thomistic Concept of the Just Price
